newsitem.title: UK: ACPC puts world 97/98 coffee output lower at 97 ml.
newsitem.headline: ACPC puts world 97/98 coffee output lower at 97 ml.

text.p: The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) forecast world coffee production to fall to 97.65 million bags in 1997/98 from a revised 98.40 million in 1996/97.
The 14-member group said in its latest monthly report that coffee was heading into a deficit of about 1.5 million bags in 1997/98 even if world consumption falls to 99 million.
It put world coffee exports at 76.80 million in 1997/98 (July/June) under a free market environment, down from 78.30 million expected in 1996/97.
The ACPC report was distributed to the delegates at its council meeting in London last week but was only made public on Tuesday.

The London-based group, led by Brazil, revised upwards its forecast for production in 1996/97 to 98.40 million from 97.28 million previously to reflect better-than-expected crops in Brazil, Peru, Indonesia and parts of Central America.
Exportable production was seen at 74.02 million in 1996/97, it said, without giving the comparative 1995/96 data.
Of the 1997/98 production, robusta's share will drop to 32.7 percent from 33.6 percent in 1996/97.
The ACPC left its 1997/98 crop estimate unchanged at 24 million bags as weather conditions had been ideal since January.
Recent estimates were still within a wide range of between 18 and 27 million, with the government numbers in the lower end of the range.
Colombian production should return to about 11.5 to 12 million bags from 1996/97's revised forecast of 10.2 million.
Robusta's production could fall to 31.95 million from 33.14 million in 1996/97 due to weather problems in Indonesia and tree stress in Ivory Coast.
The ACPC cautioned that most of the more forward-looking projections would simply cease to be relevant if there were to be a moderate and severe frost in Brazil this year.
On the demand side, it said even if world consumption falls to 99 million bags, "we still have approximately a 1.5 million deficit next year."
For this season, exports were developing into a surplus of 2.5 to 3.0 million bags with shipments running at 78 million on an annualised basis.
But the ACPC said despite the higher prices, the economic background to consumption was not all bad.

Parts of Eastern Europe, for example, is seeing its first significant growth rate for a decade, although the rate of price rises is expected to push the the trend towards arabicas in most countries into a temporary reverse.
For the coming 1997/97 (July/June) season, shipments could reach 76.80 million bags under a free market environment.
The ACPC agreed at the meeting last week to extend its export quota and limit members exports to 52.75 million bags for 12 months from July 1. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
